title: Why Your Preschooler's Hitting, Biting, or Kicking Isn't Bad Behavior—It's a Bid for Bodily Autonomy
dek: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to shout, "I have no say"—when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior will decrease.
why: Most approaches repeat "no hitting" plus punishment, without touching the need behind the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal and demonstrates scripts and case examples for negotiating with teachers.
who: Parents whose child just started preschool and who often get calls about incidents; and preschool teachers who want to reduce aggression in their classroom without relying on punishment.
skip: After 16:57 it's a course pitch; skip if you only want the methods.

points.h: A child who hits is saying: my body isn't mine
points.body: Preschool is often the first place where a child's body is controlled by an adult other than their parents for nearly every arrangement: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak, when to move. In the previous three years, they could largely decide when to run and when to go to the bathroom. Sitting on the carpet for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old lacks the language to assert "my body, my say." Hitting and kicking become one of the few tools left. So when you get that call from the teacher, don't rush to scold "keep your hands to yourself." Instead ask: how much say did this child have over their own life before this, and what can we give back?

points.h: Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
points.body: Teachers often say a preschool has a high percentage of children who are kindergarten-ready, but the core definition of that readiness is compliance: when the teacher says sit, you sit—even if you're mid-activity, even if your body is overloaded. Parents worry that if the child doesn't comply now, they won't get into a good elementary school, college, or life. But the price the child pays for this definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either; they themselves need competence, child safety, ease, and even the satisfaction of power. Many entered education to repair their own childhood wounds, but only know how to use a power-over model of relationship. Seeing both sides' positions opens up room for negotiation.

points.h: We accommodate ourselves, but refuse to accommodate our children
points.body: If adults feel overloaded at a party, we arrive early, leave early, retreat to a quiet room, or even wear noise-canceling earplugs—we find this natural. But when it comes to children, aside from routine accommodations like extra time on tests, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, and he won't survive in the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow their children. The original text offers a vivid image: a bigger, stronger adult picks you up without explanation and carries you from a quiet room back to the middle of a noisy party—if that happened to an adult, you'd immediately see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; but when it happens to a child, we look away.

points.h: The fix lies before the behavior, not in the behavior itself
points.body: Repeating "no hitting" doesn't work because that's not the knowledge the child lacks. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before the bite? What else happened earlier that day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets pushed in line may lose control—so let them stand at the front, back, or outside the line. A child who has trouble transitioning needs a few minutes' warning. Analogy to adults: when your partner snaps at you in the evening over nothing, it's often not about the immediate words but about the morning argument, lack of sleep, and a cascade of stress. If the other person then says "your attitude needs adjusting," you'd explode too; yet we often only do the latter to our children.

points.h: Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, listen to the 'no'
points.body: Telling the teacher "please change your approach" will almost certainly hit a wall. A safer opening is to set aside judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's at fault, but what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you've figured out whether the trigger is sensory or about autonomy, then empathize with the three things behind the teacher's behavior: competence, child safety, and the need for a breather. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "Can the child sit on a ball outside the circle?" If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal but the "no"—what need is the teacher still protecting? Find a way that meets both needs.

Jen's daughter Carys, at age three, couldn't nap. The teacher required her to lie down, and she was bored and frustrated—her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state regulations required offering a nap, and nap time was also the teacher's break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could play quietly with soft toys that didn't roll, while the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the break, and Jen escaped the dilemma of tattletale calls. This example shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is preserved.

points.h: All methods boil down to one question
points.body: Compress all the above methods into one sentence: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and instead ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting, and kicking are surface signals; the real message might be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meet it can be designed; and it's almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is easier than changing the child.

terms.def: The basic need to have choice over one's life and body and to act according to one's own will.
A metric used in early childhood education to measure a child's maturity in sitting still, following instructions, and adapting to group rules.
A change to the environment, rules, or arrangements to match an individual's sensory or other needs.
An interaction pattern where the adult is in a superior position and treats the child with commands and domination, as opposed to a collaborative model.

quotes.text: hitting or kicking can be one of the only tools that a three or four-year-old has for saying I don't have any say over what happens to my body right now and I need some of that.
When we imagine it happening to an adult we can kind of see it's an obvious violation of that person's body autonomy. And it is for a child too, it's just that we don't see it that way.
Being kindergarten ready means the child has learned that they are to do what an adult says even if that goes against what they know is right for their body.

But when we think about accommodations for kids unless it's for something like more time when they're taking a test we worry that they won't be able to survive in the real world if we accommodate them too much.
We know that we want that for ourselves, but somehow when kids are involved, we only focus on the behavior that we don't want to see and how do we change that?
And if the teacher says no, which they may do, what you're really listening for is what need they're trying to meet that underlies that no.
What need is this behavior communicating? Because from there you can find strategies to meet everyone's needs.
